# Goal

The workflow has two parts. Estimate point elevations from observed differences if needed. Then use known elevations to calculate terrain variables. The CTFS quadrat metrics remain useful for comparing results with published work.

Here, CTFS is Richard Condit's original distribution of scripts, `ctfs` is the R package, and `fgeo` is the later family of packages. Sources reviewed include the [CTFS archive in fgeo2](https://github.com/gabrielareto/fgeo2/tree/c16e235/evaluation/Condit/topography), [`ctfs` at `cc32c7c`](https://github.com/forestgeo/ctfs/tree/cc32c7c2a3959ef60b13144f956e99d3a0515322), [`fgeo.analyze` at `d69bfe7`](https://github.com/forestgeo/fgeo.analyze/tree/d69bfe711263305fcbaf322d402eba2f1edfb084), and [fgeo2 at `c16e235`](https://github.com/gabrielareto/fgeo2/tree/c16e235/06_topography_habitat/R). ImageJ and coordinate recovery have a [separate evaluation](5-imagej-and-geometry.qmd).

I ran the checks below with R 4.5.0 and FNN 1.1.4.1. The chunks are disabled for rendering. Run them from the repository root or the `evaluation` directory.

# Point elevations from observed differences

`solvetopo.r` uses signed elevation differences between pairs of points. Each difference is the elevation at the destination minus the elevation at the origin. The output is an estimated elevation per point ID. Join the IDs to the point coordinates to obtain an elevation table. Raster construction is a separate step. [CTFS survey script](https://github.com/gabrielareto/fgeo2/blob/c16e235/evaluation/Condit/topography/solvetopo.r)

## Core function

**`solve.topo()`** fixes one point elevation and estimates the others by equal-weight least squares. Repeated observations enter separately. The code forms a dense system and computes its inverse. A single reference point is sufficient when all points are connected by observations. [CTFS solver](https://github.com/gabrielareto/fgeo2/blob/c16e235/evaluation/Condit/topography/solvetopo.r#L46)

**Known issues.** A nonzero `baseelev` is applied only to the reference row. The other estimates are still relative to zero. The function also rebuilds the input in a fixed column order and then indexes it using the original column positions. Swapping the first two columns can reverse the estimated differences. [fgeo2 solver](https://github.com/gabrielareto/fgeo2/blob/c16e235/06_topography_habitat/R/new/topography-solvetopo.r#L25)

## Helpers

- **`rearrangeSurveyData()`** assigns a point ID to each distinct coordinate pair. It returns a coordinate lookup table and a table of observations indexed by point ID. It uses `match.dataframe()` from utilities. [CTFS helper](https://github.com/gabrielareto/fgeo2/blob/c16e235/evaluation/Condit/topography/solvetopo.r#L165)
- **`getTopoLinks()`** assembles the incoming or outgoing observations for one point. It provides the counts and signed differences used to fill the solver's system. [CTFS helper](https://github.com/gabrielareto/fgeo2/blob/c16e235/evaluation/Condit/topography/solvetopo.r#L115)

## Small check

For a chain with two elevation differences of 2 and 3 m, the results should be `0, 2, 5` at datum zero and `100, 102, 105` at datum 100. The current solver returns `100, 2, 5` at datum 100. Swapping the input columns at datum zero gives `0, -2, -5`.

```{r}
#| eval: false
path <- if (dir.exists("06_topography_habitat")) "." else ".."
current <- new.env()
sys.source(file.path(path, "06_topography_habitat/R/new/topography-solvetopo.r"), current)

survey <- data.frame(pt1 = c("1", "2"), pt2 = c("2", "3"), htdiff = c(2, 3))
rbind(
  zero = current$solve.topo(survey)$elev,
  datum = current$solve.topo(survey, baseelev = 100)$elev,
  reordered = current$solve.topo(survey[c("pt2", "pt1", "htdiff")])$elev
)
```

# Calculation of topographic variables

- **Mean elevation.** Mean of the four corner elevations of a square quadrat.
- **Slope.** Mean inclination in degrees across the four planes formed by taking three corners at a time. `quadslope()` also gives the SD across those inclinations.
- **Convexity.** Mean elevation of the focal quadrat minus the mean of the eight surrounding quadrat means, including diagonals. On the perimeter, `edgecorrect = TRUE` uses measured center elevation minus the corner mean. With `FALSE`, it uses the available neighbors. Negative values indicate concavity under the chosen rule.
- **Facet direction and slope.** Direction in radians and slope on a tangent scale for each of the eight triangular facets in a 3 × 3 elevation window.

## Core functions

- **`allquadratslopes()`** calculates `meanelev`, `convex`, and `slope` for square quadrats. CTFS finds neighbors with `findborderquads()`. fgeo2 builds the grid with `make_quadrats_fast()` and finds neighbors with `FNN`. fgeo2 checks for one center record per perimeter quadrat when edge correction is requested. It still fills the corner matrix in input row order and returns metrics without quadrat IDs. The grid constructor can produce clipped quadrats, while the calculation filters coordinates by exact multiples of the nominal side and uses that side in the slope formula. The method assumes full aligned squares. [CTFS function](https://github.com/gabrielareto/fgeo2/blob/c16e235/evaluation/Condit/topography/slope.r#L100) · [fgeo2 function](https://github.com/gabrielareto/fgeo2/blob/c16e235/06_topography_habitat/R/new/topography-slope.r#L49) · [Grid constructor](https://github.com/gabrielareto/fgeo2/blob/c16e235/03_spatial/R/new/quadrats.R#L252)
- **`calc.gradient()`** assembles the eight facet results. It treats matrix rows as `x` and columns as `y`, the reverse of the elevation readers. It reads `[2, 3]` twice and skips `[3, 2]`. Changing the skipped cell leaves the result identical. The code stops at facet geometry. The cited method also routes flow and accumulates upslope area. [Facet code](https://github.com/gabrielareto/fgeo2/blob/c16e235/06_topography_habitat/R/new/topography-slope.r#L232) · [Seibert and McGlynn 2007](https://doi.org/10.1029/2006WR005128)

## Helpers

- **`readelevdata()`** reads a table or a tab-delimited file and fills an elevation matrix. It assumes a complete regular grid starting at zero, sorted by `x` and then `y`. Shuffling the input can silently place elevations at the wrong coordinates. [CTFS reader](https://github.com/gabrielareto/fgeo2/blob/c16e235/evaluation/Condit/topography/slope.r#L20)
- **`elev.to.list()`** returns the table and a matrix built with the same ordering assumption. `allquadratslopes()` uses the table and builds its own matrix. [CTFS converter](https://github.com/gabrielareto/fgeo2/blob/c16e235/evaluation/Condit/topography/slope.r#L57)
- **`quadslope()`** calls `calcslope()` for each set of three corners and returns the mean and SD. `allquadratslopes()` uses the mean. [CTFS quadrat slope](https://github.com/gabrielareto/fgeo2/blob/c16e235/evaluation/Condit/topography/slope.r#L192)
- **`calcslope()`** calculates the inclination of a plane through three points forming a right isosceles triangle in plan view. It assumes one shared horizontal length for the two short sides. [CTFS triangle slope](https://github.com/gabrielareto/fgeo2/blob/c16e235/evaluation/Condit/topography/slope.r#L237)
- **`calc.directionslope()`** calculates a single facet's direction and slope from coordinate and elevation differences. The flat case yields a direction of zero even though a flat facet has no defined downhill direction. [CTFS facet helper](https://github.com/gabrielareto/fgeo2/blob/c16e235/evaluation/Condit/topography/slope.r#L363)

## Small checks

### Corner elevations, row order, and perimeter

A plane on a 5 m grid gives four equal slopes of about 74.50°. Swapping just two input rows changes the first quadrat mean from 112.5 to 125 and its slope from 74.50° to 81.16°. Default edge correction stops on this corner-only grid. The last check shows that changing the omitted cell in the facet calculation has no effect.

```{r}
#| eval: false
path <- if (dir.exists("06_topography_habitat")) "." else ".."
current <- new.env()
sys.source(file.path(path, "06_topography_habitat/R/new/topography-slope.r"), current)
sys.source(file.path(path, "03_spatial/R/new/quadrats.R"), current)

grid <- expand.grid(y = seq(0, 10, 5), x = seq(0, 10, 5))
grid$elev <- 100 + 2 * grid$x + 3 * grid$y
shuffled <- grid[c(9, 2:8, 1), ]

a <- current$allquadratslopes(list(col = grid), 5, c(10, 10), edgecorrect = FALSE)
b <- current$allquadratslopes(list(col = shuffled), 5, c(10, 10), edgecorrect = FALSE)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(a$slope, rep(atan(sqrt(13)) * 180 / pi, 4))))
cbind(a[1, ], b[1, ])

try(current$allquadratslopes(list(col = grid), 5, c(10, 10)))

facet <- matrix(0, 3, 3)
changed <- facet
changed[3, 2] <- 10
identical(current$calc.gradient(facet), current$calc.gradient(changed))
```

### Agreement on one real grid

With ordered Luquillo elevations and the legacy perimeter rule, archived CTFS and current fgeo2 give identical mean elevation, slope, and convexity across all 400 quadrats. I loaded the archived `fgeo.x` data directly for this check. The survey spacing is 5 m and the quadrats are 20 m. [Elevation data](https://github.com/forestgeo/fgeo.x/blob/64e9a4be80c84518223a87a45901e4a056b71bc8/data/elevation.rda)

```{r}
#| eval: false
legacy <- new.env()
sys.source(file.path(path, "evaluation/Condit/topography/slope.r"), legacy)
sys.source(file.path(path, "evaluation/Condit/spatial/quadfunc.r"), legacy)
elevation <- fgeo.x::elevation
elevation$col <- as.data.frame(elevation$col)
plot.dim <- c(elevation$xdim, elevation$ydim)

a <- legacy$allquadratslopes(elevation, 20, plot.dim, edgecorrect = TRUE)
b <- current$allquadratslopes(elevation, 20, plot.dim, edgecorrect = TRUE)
stopifnot(nrow(b) == 400L, identical(a, b))
```

# What ctfs and fgeo add

- **`ctfs`** adds package documentation and exports. Nine of the ten function bodies are identical to CTFS, counting `solve.topo()` under its new name `solve_topo()`. `allquadratslopes()` adds a warning for a missing `col` element and changes the indexing used to look up perimeter midpoints. Both versions gave identical results on a synthetic grid under both edge rules. `solve_topo()` retains the datum and column-order bugs. [`ctfs` terrain source](https://github.com/forestgeo/ctfs/blob/cc32c7c2a3959ef60b13144f956e99d3a0515322/R/slope.R#L257) · [`ctfs` survey source](https://github.com/forestgeo/ctfs/blob/cc32c7c2a3959ef60b13144f956e99d3a0515322/R/solvetopo.R#L123)
- **`fgeo`** loads the package suite. `fgeo.analyze::fgeo_topography()` uses the same formulas in its own copy of the code. It accepts an elevation table or ForestGEO list, adds `gx` and `gy` to the output, and adds some checks. The input row-order assumption remains. The warning about missing midpoint elevations can still be followed by an error. In the Tian Tong case, `edgecorrect = FALSE` worked. The package tests give cases for comparison. [Source](https://github.com/forestgeo/fgeo.analyze/blob/d69bfe711263305fcbaf322d402eba2f1edfb084/R/fgeo_topography.R) · [Tests](https://github.com/forestgeo/fgeo.analyze/blob/d69bfe711263305fcbaf322d402eba2f1edfb084/tests/testthat/test-fgeo_topography.R) · [Tian Tong report](https://github.com/forestgeo/fgeo.tool/issues/59)
- **Related tools.** `fgeo.tool::fgeo_elevation()` standardizes elevation tables, and `extract_from_habitat.R` infers grid size and plot dimensions. `fgeo.plot` draws contours, as does `maptopo()` in fgeo2. `fgeo_habitat()` clusters the terrain metrics. Sampling arbitrary layers at points or summarizing them over polygons belongs in the environmental extraction workflow. [Elevation tables](https://github.com/forestgeo/fgeo.tool/blob/main/R/fgeo_elevation.R) · [Grid dimensions](https://github.com/forestgeo/fgeo.tool/blob/main/R/extract_from_habitat.R) · [Contours](https://github.com/forestgeo/fgeo.plot/blob/main/R/plot_sp_elev-implementation.R#L142) · [fgeo2 mapping scripts](https://github.com/gabrielareto/fgeo2/tree/c16e235/07_mapping_plotting/R/new) · [Habitat assignment](https://github.com/forestgeo/fgeo.analyze/blob/master/R/fgeo_habitat.R#L42)

The CTFS scripts are the reference for the calculations. The package sources add interface details and test cases for this evaluation.

# Uses in practice

| Use | Evidence |
|---|---|
| **Adjust a survey and draw contours.** | The CTFS Manaus tutorial uses a real 49 ha survey. It calls `rearrangeSurveyData()` and `solve.topo()`, sorts the resulting elevations by coordinates, and plots contours. Condit (1998) gives the least-squares calculation and an Ituri example. Interpolation is a separate step. [CTFS tutorial, sections 1–4](https://ctfs.si.edu/Public/CTFSRPackage/files/tutorials/topography/) · [Condit 1998, ch. 2.1](https://forestgeo.si.edu/sites/default/files/condit_1998_censusplotsmethodsbook.pdf) |
| **Describe habitats with the legacy metrics.** | Sinharaja used elevation, slope, and convexity to define eight habitats. The paper gives both convexity rules. At Ailaoshan, Song et al. report using the CTFS R package for 20 m terrain variables and use terrain for habitat classes and as continuous covariates in a seedling recruitment study. The paper gives the methods but no individual function names. [Gunatilleke et al. 2006, Methods and Fig. 2](https://ctfs.si.edu/Public/pdfs/Gunatilleke_etal_2006_JTropEcol.pdf) · [Song et al. 2018, sections 2.2.3 and 2.3](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.foreco.2018.07.038) |
| **Combine terrain and soil at different scales.** | At Tyson, four terrain variables and 13 soil variables were used to describe a continuous environmental gradient. The analysis used 20 m quadrats for adults and saplings, and 10 m subquadrats for seeds and seedlings. [LaManna et al. 2016, Supplemental Methods, p. 1](https://repository.si.edu/bitstreams/7354160e-6174-480d-a3ef-b212341e223f/download) |
| **Summarize a DEM around individual trees.** | A Luquillo study used a 1 m DEM to summarize elevation, slope, curvature, and wetness in 20 m radius buffers around trees. The resulting variables are available in the study data. This is a direct use of terrain layers with a different spatial unit. [Ankori-Karlinsky et al. 2025, Methods, “Tree architecture”](https://doi.org/10.1111/nph.70294) · [Data and README](https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.zw3r228fq) |

The `fgeo.analyze` habitat tutorial builds classes with `fgeo_habitat()` and then uses the map in `tt_test()`. The papers and tutorials above show why the calculations matter. The tutorial calls and Song et al.'s package attribution are direct evidence of code use. The other papers document the methods or the resulting variables. [`fgeo.analyze` habitat tutorial](https://forestgeo.github.io/fgeo.analyze/articles/siteonly/tt_test.html)

# Design of future code

## One function for point elevations

Proposed interface `estimate_point_elevations(x_i, y_i, x_j, y_j, dz)`. Each observation gives two coordinate pairs and `dz = z_j - z_i`. Return one `{x, y, z}` row per distinct point. Solve the anchored equal-weight least-squares problem directly. Allow a known reference point and elevation. For relative elevations, set a point selected by a fixed coordinate rule to zero so the result is independent of input order. Reject disconnected observations when using a single reference. [fgeo2 design principles](../README.md#design-principles)

## Tutorial using standard R tools

1. **Optional survey adjustment.** Show how to go from paired coordinates and elevation differences to `{x, y, z}`. Compare fitted differences with the original observations to check the survey.
2. **Build or load a DEM.** Check duplicates, gaps, spacing, and units in a regular coordinate table. Index by coordinates and show how the points map to cell centers. Keep plot bounds and the coordinate system explicit, including when coordinates are plot-local. Treat interpolation as a separate choice for irregular or incomplete surveys. Users with an existing DEM start here. [`terra::rast()`](https://rspatial.github.io/terra/reference/rast.html) · [`gstat::krige()`](https://r-spatial.github.io/gstat/reference/krige.html)
3. **Calculate terrain variables.** Use standard package calls directly. Cover slope, aspect, northness, eastness, topographic position, ruggedness, and curvature. State the method, units, and neighborhood. Specify the reference direction for aspect and leave aspect undefined on flats. Show a table-based calculation when its definition uses point elevations, such as mean elevation at quadrat corners. Keep DEM-based slope and topographic position distinct from the CTFS quadrat definitions. Give wetness a separate example. Calculate specific contributing area before clipping the DEM to the plot, and document flow routing and the treatment of depressions and flats. [`terra::terrain()`](https://rspatial.github.io/terra/reference/terrain.html) · [WhiteboxTools wetness index](https://jblindsay.github.io/wbt_book/available_tools/geomorphometric_analysis.html#wetnessindex) · [Contributing area and edge effects](https://hydrology.usu.edu/taudem/taudem5/help53/DInfinityContributingArea.html)
4. **Combine with other environmental layers.** Use named `SpatRaster` layers and GeoTIFF for saved rasters. Stack layers that share their extent, origin, resolution, and coordinate reference system. Layers on different grids can stay on their native grids for later extraction to common points or polygons. Use those layers for visualization in `07_mapping_plotting`. [`terra::compareGeom()`](https://rspatial.github.io/terra/reference/compareGeom.html) · [`terra::writeRaster()`](https://rspatial.github.io/terra/reference/writeRaster.html) · [OGC GeoTIFF](https://www.ogc.org/standards/geotiff/)

Use small flat, planar, and curved surfaces to check units, orientation, and method differences. The archived CTFS code remains available for comparisons with the original definitions. [Topography issue #13](https://github.com/gabrielareto/fgeo2/issues/13) · [Habitat issue #12](https://github.com/gabrielareto/fgeo2/issues/12)
